S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention—such as disorganization, distractibility, and forgetfulness—without the prominent overt hyperactivity seen in the combined type. Symptoms must begin in childhood, be present in at least two settings, persist for at least six months, and cause clinically significant impairment in social, academic, or occupational functioning. In adults, it often presents as chronic difficulties with planning, sustaining focus on tasks, managing time, and following through, rather than overt behavioral disruption. It can be misattributed to anxiety, depression, or personality traits, so course since childhood, pervasiveness across contexts, and a longstanding history of similar difficulties help distinguish it from other conditions or purely situational stress reactions.

patient.personality: Lazaro is a hyper‑organized, curiosity‑driven community organizer who loves art and learning but is prone to intense anxiety and occasional impulsive splurges on creative projects.
patient.stressor: After finishing high school and attempting a few part‑time jobs, Lazaro decided to focus on building art‑driven community projects and exploring further education options, moving from the clear structure of school into a self‑directed schedule. Without the external deadlines and daily routines that had previously masked his lifelong tendency to drift off during mentally demanding tasks, he suddenly had to generate his own sustained focus for grant applications, long‑form reading, and planning complex events. Over the next year, he noticed that while he could spend hours on photography or cooking, he repeatedly put off paperwork, avoided dense reading related to mental‑health programming, and hopped between ideas instead of pushing through the more cognitively demanding parts of his projects, leading to missed opportunities and stalled initiatives. Feeling frustrated that his carefully designed Trello boards and planning rituals still weren’t enough to help him sit with sustained mental effort, and worried that this pattern was holding back both his career and his community work, he sought a psychiatric evaluation to understand why he kept dodging any task that required prolonged concentration.
patient.chief_complaint: “Any time I have to sit and really concentrate on something for a while, I end up avoiding it or bouncing away from it.”

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: Even though I love making these super detailed Trello boards for my community art projects, when it’s time to actually break things down into steps—like who to email first, what to do this week, what can wait—I just kind of freeze, bounce between tasks, and end up doing random easy things while the important stuff gets pushed to the last minute or dropped completely.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: Anything that means sitting still and thinking hard for a long stretch—like reading a 10‑page grant guideline or drafting a proposal—feels so heavy and uncomfortable that I keep finding excuses to make tea, check Instagram, or reorganize my photo files instead of actually starting it.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: I’m constantly misplacing practical stuff I need for projects—like the notebook with all my workshop ideas or the USB drive with my photo files—and I’ll swear I just had it in my hand, then spend twenty minutes tearing through my backpack and desk while getting more and more annoyed with myself.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: When I try to focus on something mentally demanding, like reading research on mental‑health programs, the smallest thing—a car outside, a notification on my phone, or even a random idea for a mural—pulls me completely off track before I even realize I’ve stopped paying attention.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: Despite having everything in my calendar, I still forget basic stuff like calling people back about venue bookings, sending follow‑up emails, or paying my phone bill on time, and I usually only remember when someone reminds me or I get a warning message.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: Whenever I’m in a meeting or sitting at my desk trying to concentrate, I notice I’m constantly tapping my foot, rolling a pen between my fingers, or shifting around in the chair without really meaning to, and I only catch it when someone looks at me or the noise starts to bug me.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
S011.manifestation: In longer meetings or workshops where I’m supposed to stay seated, I usually end up getting up under the excuse of refilling my water or checking something on the wall because I just feel too restless to sit still the whole time.
